learning_objective: 🎯 Enjoy a humorous and ironic poem criticizing foolish governance, blind justice, and a society that values peace over competent leadership.

key_vocabulary.hindi_meaning: हस्तक्षेप न करने की नीति (जो हो रहा है, होने दो)

main_concepts.simple_explanation: A 'just and placid' king orders an arch to be built. When riding under it, the arch is too low and knocks off his crown. Angry, the king orders the chief of builders to be hanged.

The chief of builders blames the workmen. The workmen blame the bricks/masons. The masons blame the architect. The architect reminds the king that the king himself had changed the architectural plans!

Confused, the king calls the oldest, 'wisest' man in the city. The old man logically says the Arch itself is the culprit and must be hanged. But a councillor objects to hanging something that touched the king's crown.
The crowd wants a hanging. The noose is set up, but it's set too high. Only one man is tall enough to fit the noose perfectly—the King himself. So, the king is hanged by his own decree.

According to custom, the first person to pass the city gates gets to name the next king. An idiot passes by. Since he answers 'Melon' to every question, a Melon is crowned King. The public is happy because the Melon doesn't interfere with their lives.

fun_activity.title: 🍉 The Melon Test
fun_activity.instructions: Ask a friend to name the best leader in the world. When they give a serious answer, reply: 'I think a Watermelon is better. It's sweet, silent, and doesn't charge taxes!' You've just explained the philosophy of Laissez-faire!

exam_tips: 📌 The poem is a sharp satire on foolish rulers and blind adherence to customs/rules.
📌 The phrase 'just and placid' is used ironically. The king is neither fair (he orders random hangings) nor calm (he gets angry easily).
📌 Why did the people accept a melon? Because they believed in 'laissez-faire'—they wanted peace and non-interference, regardless of who ruled.
quick_recap: ⭐ The poem is written by Vikram Seth in a ballad format (storytelling poem).
⭐ The cycle of blame exposes the incompetence of the entire administrative system.
⭐ The public's indifference at the end shows a society that cares only about its own comfort.
